intake: believer - Roman Catholic, Sunday Mass every week, confession a few times a year, rosary most evenings; came to philosophy late and I want arguments to say what they mean.

walk.note: That is how it happened to me: my parents handed me the faith before I could ask for it. 'Story' is a thin word for it, but the move is honest.
Aquinas argued from motion and causes and he was a friar, so looking for God in the world is not leaving religion; still, the destination is my own position, so I go.

Classical theism does not deny a personal God; Aquinas's God has intellect and will, and the First Cause acts at every instant by holding things in being. The either/or is built on a wrong description.
The premise that a God who acts must show up as a measurable prayer effect treats God like a medicine in a trial; no Catholic ever claimed prayer works that way.
Granting atheism for the sake of argument, I agree the mind does not look like it reduces to matter, and I believe in the soul anyway.

That everything the mind does depends on the brain and changes with it shows the mind uses the brain, not that it is nothing but brain; dependence is not identity. The soul as form of the body is not a ghost pushing a machine.
Granting materialism, widening 'matter' to whatever physics describes is just tidying the word.
Physicalism says everything is physical; Dream says everything is mind. 'Physics describes structure, not what has it' is a gap in physicalism, not a reason to flip to its opposite.
A dream needs a dreamer, yes. I would say the dreamer could be God, but the route ruled Him out earlier and I am granting that.
Others have brains and faces like mine; of course they are subjects.
I take it gladly. For me mercy is not only a choice but a command received, but the move still carries me.
Caring before you have proof does mean admitting what you do not know; Augustine and Cusa are good company. The sentence about entropy I could not follow, but it is not load-bearing.
Hope is where I live, so I take it. But the real move is one line, 'choose hope', and the rest of the paragraph about fungible goods and Parfit is a second argument hidden inside the first.
That God knows all in one act, not step by step, is exactly what I was taught.
'More of a bargain than an argument' is all the text gives. A bargain with whom, for what? I cannot tell what is being claimed.

'To think is to ignore' is true of my mind, not of every possible mind; the move itself admits Aquinas's non-discursive knowing has not been shown incoherent, so the premise is stated as false by the author's own hand.
Granting no maker, suffering is still bad for the one who suffers; I agree with that much. I am the critic who asks what grounds it.
The text says the need to be remembered is a motive for asking, not evidence of what the self is. A motive does not carry you to a position; it only makes you want one.
There is nothing here to take; the author is waiting for data from a machine that does not exist. I would not wait there. I would go back to Religion₂ and stay.

first_exit.why: The move says classical theism denies a personal God and that a first cause is not a God who acts. Both are wrong about Aquinas: his God has intellect and will, and sustains every creature at every moment, so the dilemma 'not all-powerful or a subject' never gets off the ground for me.

comment: Mercy is the hinge of your whole map, and you treat it as something you chose on your own against uncertainty; in my city 'Jezu, ufam Tobie' is painted on walls, and for us mercy is the center too, but it is received before it is chosen. Your first turn leaves God on a wrong description of Aquinas at move 3, and your second turn leaves Him at move 16 on a premise you yourself say has not been shown, so twice you walk out through a door you admit is not properly shut. Say what each move claims in one plain sentence first, then give the reasons; move 13 made me read it three times.
